notes.1bi: Very few candidates were able to describe the change in the appearance of the magnesium from silver or grey to a white ash or recognise that it would burn. Common references to the magnesium melting, turning black or darkening scored no credit. Vague answers such as ‘changes colour’ were prevalent.
notes.1bii: Able candidates realised that the product formed would be alkaline and turn the Universal Indicator blue or purple. References to the formation of an acid and colour changes to red or yellow were seen and scored no credit.
notes.1c: Generally well answered. Many candidates identified the formation of hydrogen and a positive test for the gas. Credit was awarded for the gas catching fire, exploding or popping with the lighted splint.
notes.2a: Most candidates labelled the lines correctly and realised that twice as much gas was formed in Experiment 2.
notes.2bi: Most candidates stated that water should be added to dilute the acid further. However, many candidates did not specify the relative amounts of acid and water to be mixed and only scored partial credit. Good answers specified equal volumes of acid and water to be mixed. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0620 Chemistry June 2014
notes.2bii: The sketch curve for Experiment 3 showed good differentiation. Able candidates realised that the curve would be less steep and level out at 15 cm .
notes.2c: Many diagrams were left blank or completed so that they would not work. More able candidates used a measuring cylinder filled with water or a gas syringe. References to distillation and condensers, and test-tubes in closed systems were common and it was apparent that many candidates had never experienced this practical procedure.
notes.2d: Well answered. Most answers referred to heating or using a catalyst. Full credit was rarely given as explanations were often missing.
notes.3a: Electroplating was often recognised and credit was given for electrolysis.
notes.3b: The idea of removing impurities was common but the reason for doing so was often omitted. Candidates often did not state that the key was rubbed with sandpaper so that an even coating of nickel on the key would result.
notes.3c: More able learners named a nickel salt and used an aqueous solution of the salt. A range of incorrect answers such as copper sulfate, silver nitrate, acids and water showed a lack of knowledge and understanding.
notes.3d: Observations scoring no credit referred to the key getting bigger or smaller, gases evolved or colour changes. The bulb lighting up or a silver deposit on the key were specific expected observations.
notes.3e: The majority of responses scored credit for using water and some form of heat or absorbent e.g. a paper towel.
notes.4a: & (b) The tables of results were completed correctly by the vast majority of candidates.
notes.4d: Most candidates plotted the points on the grid correctly. The majority of candidates drew smooth line graphs but others joined the points with straight lines drawn with a ruler. Some graphs were not labelled.
notes.4ei: Most candidates identified the temperature after 45 seconds and scored full credit. Some errors in reading the scale were evident. The question asked candidates to show clearly on the graph how they worked out their answer. A minority of candidates did not follow this instruction and could not be credited
notes.4eii: The scale on the x -axis was sometimes misread and tie lines were often not evident.
notes.4f: The type of chemical process was usually correctly identified as endothermic. Some confused responses mentioned exothermic.
notes.4g: More able candidates concluded that a carbonate was present or referred to carbon dioxide gas. Many candidates missed the point and made vague references to reactions happening or metals being involved.
notes.4h: Most candidates erroneously thought that a larger volume of water would result in a faster reaction and/or larger temperature change. Better candidates realised that the temperature changes would be lower because of the larger volume of water.
notes.4hi: Many candidates realised that the temperature of the solution would return to the initial temperature of 25 C or room temperature. Many failed to explain that this was because the reaction would be finished. Vague answers were seen such as ‘the temperature will decrease’ or ‘heat would be lost to the environment’.
notes.4j: Most candidates scored credit for realising that more results, readings or points on the graph would result. Reference to accuracy was allowed as an advantage. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0620 Chemistry June 2014
notes.5ci: A white precipitate insoluble in excess aqueous sodium hydroxide was generally well known. Some candidates thought that the precipitate would be soluble. Additional incorrect observations such as effervescence meant credit could not always be given.
notes.5cii: The incorrect observation that a white precipitate formed was frequently seen.
notes.5ciii: Some candidates realised that a yellow precipitate would be formed.
notes.5d: Meaningful conclusions were variable. The presence of copper oxide was given by the more able candidates for full credit though other named copper compound was a common response.
